rendered:
The short answer is no: none of these papers covers this. None of them tests ethylene glycol mixed with polyethylene glycol, and none recovers critical materials from magnets. Searches for these terms found nothing anywhere in the collection.[1] Magnets come up only in passing, as an end use of cobalt. A paper on cobalt-free cathodes lists it among alloys, catalysts, magnets, and pigments.[2] A review on cobalt-free cathodes lists magnets, super alloys, and pigments[3]. The only polyethylene glycol (PEG) in the collection is part of a polymer coating on cathode particles (PANI-PEG coating[4]). It is not used as a solvent for extraction.

What the collection does show is ethylene glycol on its own, used on spent lithium-ion batteries:
- A paper on direct recycling describes peeling electrode materials off their metal foils as an enabling step toward recovering critical materials from spent[5] lithium-ion batteries. It uses ethylene glycol without any additives[6] to break the bond between the PVDF binder and the current collector. In that paper, ethylene glycol separates the electrode materials quickly, leaves their crystal structure and morphology unchanged, and can be reused. However, this is a physical delamination step. The metals themselves are not extracted.[7][8][9]
- A review in the collection reports actual leaching, but with a different mixture: a deep eutectic solvent made of choline chloride and[10] ethylene glycol. It was used to recover more than 90% of cobalt[11] and lithium based compounds from the LCO cathode.[12]

So these papers support ethylene glycol-based processing only for lithium-ion battery cathodes. Whether an ethylene glycol/polyethylene glycol mixture would work on magnets would have to come from other sources.
